items.followUp: How are cathode rays produced in a discharge tube?

rubric.why: Shows how the positive ions originate.
rubric.description: Gas atoms lose electrons and form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that gas atoms become positive ions.

rubric.why: Explains how the positive rays emerge.
rubric.description: Positive ions move towards the cathode and pass through its perforations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that positive ions pass through holes in the cathode.

modelAnswer: Gas atoms in the discharge tube lose electrons and form positive ions.
These ions move towards the cathode and pass through its perforations, producing positive rays (canal rays).

rubric.description: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the properties of elements are periodic functions.

rubric.why: Gives the basis of Mendeleev's periodic law.
rubric.description: The periodicity is related to the atomic masses of the elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying atomic mass or atomic weight as the basis.

modelAnswer: Mendeleev's Periodic Law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten?

rubric.why: Identifies the ions and the strong attractions in an ionic compound.
rubric.description: Oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Explains why high temperatures are needed.
rubric.description: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome the attractions and separate the ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that considerable energy is needed to overcome the ionic attractions.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces in a crystal lattice.
A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces and separate the ions, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Define a polar covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a non-polar covalent bond by how electrons are shared.
rubric.description: The bonding pair of electrons is shared equally between the bonded atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the bonding electrons are shared equally.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: Examples include H2, Cl2, O2 and N2.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving one correct example.

modelAnswer: A non-polar covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the bonding pair of electrons is shared equally between the bonded atoms.
Examples include H2, Cl2, O2 and N2.
